tips.title: Variation comes first
tips.body: Natural selection cannot start without **variation already present**. Selection does not create the useful characteristic — it **selects from** what mutation and sexual reproduction have already produced. Getting this order right is most of the marks.

tips.title: Four steps, in order
tips.body: **Variation → competition → the best suited survive and reproduce → the alleles become more common.** Learn the chain and every natural selection question follows the same shape, whatever the organism.

tips.title: Bacteria do not become resistant because of the antibiotic
tips.body: The resistant bacteria were **already there**, by chance, from a **mutation**. The antibiotic **kills the rest**, leaving them to reproduce. Saying the antibiotic caused the resistance reverses cause and effect and loses the mark.

tips.title: Acquired characteristics are not inherited
tips.body: **Environmental variation** — a scar, learned language, muscle built by training — is **acquired** during life and is **not passed on**. Only **genetic** variation is inherited, which is why natural selection acts on genetic variation alone.

tips.title: Say "more likely to", not "in order to"
tips.body: Organisms are **more likely to survive** because of a characteristic they already had. They do not develop it **in order to** survive. Purposeful wording is the commonest way to lose evolution marks.

why.matters:
Natural selection is one of the few ideas in science that is almost obvious once stated and was very hard to arrive at. It needs only three things to be true — that organisms **vary**, that more are born than can survive, and that some of the variation is **inherited** — and then the rest follows whether anyone believes it or not.

The trap is direction. Selection does not produce the useful characteristic; it selects from variation that was already there, for reasons that had nothing to do with being useful.

examples.title: Why bacteria do not become resistant because of the antibiotic
examples.body:
It sounds like the drug provokes the resistance. It does not. A population of bacteria already **varies**, because mutations happen constantly and at random, and by chance a few are unaffected by the drug **before it arrives**.

The antibiotic then kills the rest, and the survivors reproduce — which is the four steps of natural selection running in a few days instead of a few million years. That is why resistance is the strongest everyday evidence for Darwin's theory, and why *the bacteria adapted to the antibiotic* is the wrong sentence.

visual.alt: A flow chart of natural selection in four steps: variation that is already present, competition to survive, the best suited surviving and reproducing, and their alleles becoming more common in the population

examples.title: Why a bodybuilder's children are not born strong
examples.body:
Variation comes from two places and only one of them is passed on. **Genetic** variation — from mutation and from sexual reproduction — is in the DNA of every cell, including the gametes, so it is **inherited**.

**Environmental** variation is acquired during a life: muscle built by training, a scar, a language, a suntan. None of it changes the DNA in the gametes, so none of it is passed on. That distinction is what rules out an entire earlier theory of evolution, and it is worth a mark whenever a question offers you an acquired characteristic.

visual.alt: A table of the two causes of variation: genetic variation from mutation and sexual reproduction, which is inherited, and environmental variation acquired during a life, which is not

examples.title: Why the wording of an evolution answer is marked so strictly
examples.body:
Two sentences that sound alike score very differently. *The moths became darker **in order to** hide* is wrong; *the darker moths were **more likely to** survive* is right.

The difference is not fussiness. The first says the population changed **because** it needed to, which is the theory Darwin replaced; the second says the variation was already there and the environment did the selecting. Getting the direction of causation the right way round is the whole content of the idea, so it is exactly what a mark scheme tests.

visual.alt: A table of three phrases to avoid in an evolution answer and what to write instead: more likely to rather than in order to, those that varied survived rather than they adapted, and best suited rather than strongest

steps.title: Where variation comes from
steps.body:
**The specification names two causes of variation that influence phenotype.**

**Genetic variation** — *different characteristics as a result of **mutation** and **sexual reproduction***.

**Mutations** are changes in the DNA, and they are the **original source** of new alleles. **Sexual reproduction** then shuffles those alleles into new combinations, through meiosis producing genetically different gametes and through two parents contributing.

**Environmental variation** — *different characteristics caused by an organism's **environment** (**acquired characteristics**)*.

A scar, a language learned, muscle built by training, a plant grown small because of poor soil — all acquired during the organism's life.

**The crucial difference: acquired characteristics are not inherited.** Genetic variation is passed to offspring; environmental variation is not. This is why natural selection acts on **genetic** variation alone, and it is examined directly.

**Many characteristics involve both.** Height has a strong genetic component but is also affected by nutrition. Only the genetic part is passed on.

**How much variation is there?** *There is usually **extensive genetic variation** within a population of a species, and these arise through **mutations**.*

**But most mutations do nothing.** *Most genetic mutations have **no effect** on the phenotype, **some** have a **small** effect, and **rarely**, a **single mutation will significantly affect** the phenotype.*

That balance matters. Mutations are not mainly harmful dramatic events — they are mostly silent, and the occasional useful one is what makes evolution possible.

steps.title: Darwin and Wallace
steps.body:
*(Biology only.)* **The specification asks you to describe the work of Charles Darwin and Alfred Wallace in developing the theory of evolution by natural selection, and to explain the impact of these ideas on modern biology.**

**Darwin** spent years gathering evidence, much of it on the voyage of the *Beagle*. He observed enormous **variation** within species, noticed that organisms on different islands were **suited to their particular conditions**, and studied fossils. He also drew on observations of **selective breeding**, where humans choose which organisms reproduce — which showed that characteristics in a population **can be changed** by controlling who breeds.

**Wallace** worked independently, mainly in south-east Asia, and arrived at **the same idea** of natural selection. It was his letter to Darwin, setting out essentially the same theory, that prompted Darwin to publish. Their work was presented **jointly** in 1858, and Darwin published *On the Origin of Species* the following year.

**Wallace is worth mentioning explicitly** — the specification names him, and answers that credit Darwin alone miss a mark that is simply there.

**Why the theory was slow to be accepted.** It conflicted with widely held **religious beliefs** about the creation of species, the **evidence** was still limited, and nobody knew **how characteristics were inherited** — genes and DNA were unknown, and Mendel's work was not yet recognised — so Darwin could describe **that** characteristics were inherited without being able to say **how**.

**The impact on modern biology** is that evolution by natural selection became the **unifying explanation** for the diversity of life. It explains why organisms are suited to their environments, why species are related, and why classification forms a branching pattern — and it underpins work on antibiotic resistance, pesticide resistance and conservation today.

steps.title: Antibiotic resistance
steps.body:
**The specification asks you to explain how the emergence of resistant organisms supports Darwin's theory, including antibiotic resistance in bacteria.** It is the best evidence available, because it happens fast enough to watch.

**Follow the four steps with bacteria.**

**Variation.** In a population of bacteria, a **random mutation** gives a few individuals **resistance** to an antibiotic. This happens **by chance**, and **before** the antibiotic is used.

**Competition and selection pressure.** The antibiotic is given. It is a very strong **selection pressure** — an environment in which one characteristic decides survival.

**Survival.** The **non-resistant bacteria are killed**. The **resistant ones survive**.

**Reproduction.** The survivors reproduce — bacteria very rapidly — and **pass on the allele for resistance**. The population rebuilds, and now **all of it is resistant**.

**The numbers make it vivid.** Suppose **1000** bacteria, of which **1%** — just **10** — happen to be resistant. The antibiotic kills **990**. Those 10 survivors then divide: after **7** generations there are $10 \times 2^{7} = $ **1280** bacteria — more than the original population, and **every one resistant**.

**Why this supports Darwin.** Every step of his theory is visible, and the change happens over **days** rather than millennia. It is evolution observed directly.

**The error to avoid.** The antibiotic did **not cause** the resistance. The resistant bacteria **were already there**; the antibiotic merely **removed their competition**. Saying bacteria "become resistant because of the antibiotic" reverses cause and effect, and examiners penalise it.

**Why this matters practically.** It is why antibiotics should not be over-prescribed, why courses must be **completed**, and why new antibiotics are continually needed.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Put variation first, always.** Natural selection **selects from** variation that already exists; it does not **create** the useful characteristic. Every strong answer begins with variation caused by **mutation and sexual reproduction**.

**Say "more likely to survive", never "in order to".** Organisms do not develop characteristics **for a purpose**. A characteristic arises by **chance mutation**, and if it happens to help, its owner is **more likely** to survive and reproduce. Purposeful wording — *the bacteria developed resistance to survive* — is the single commonest way to lose evolution marks.

**Get the antibiotic story the right way round.** The resistant bacteria existed **before** the antibiotic, from a **random mutation**. The antibiotic **kills the non-resistant**, removing competition. It **selects**; it does not **cause**. This is worth stating explicitly, because the wrong version is so natural to say.

**Finish the chain with inheritance.** The survivors **pass on the allele**, so the proportion with it **rises over generations**. An answer that stops at "the resistant ones survive" has left out the step that makes it evolution rather than just a cull.

**Keep acquired characteristics out.** Environmental variation — scars, learned skills, muscle from training — is **not inherited**, so it cannot be selected for. Only **genetic** variation is passed on.

*(Biology only.)* **Credit Wallace.** The specification names **Charles Darwin and Alfred Wallace**. Wallace reached the theory **independently**, and it was his letter that prompted Darwin to publish. Naming only Darwin leaves a mark unclaimed.

*(Biology only.)* **Explain why the theory was slow to be accepted.** It conflicted with the **religious beliefs** of the time, the **evidence** was still limited, and there was **no known mechanism of inheritance**, since genes and DNA were unknown and Mendel's work unrecognised. Darwin could show **that** characteristics were inherited but not **how**.

**Keep mutations in proportion.** **Most have no effect**, **some** a **small** effect, and **rarely** one significantly affects the phenotype. Mutations are the raw material of variation, not mainly a cause of disease.

**Remember evolution happens to populations.** An individual does not evolve. It is the **proportion** of individuals carrying an allele that changes across generations.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Genetic variation** comes from **mutation and sexual reproduction** — and **is inherited**.
- **Environmental variation** gives **acquired characteristics** — and is **not inherited**.
- There is usually **extensive genetic variation** in a population, arising through **mutations**.
- **Most mutations have no effect**; some a small effect; **rarely** one significantly affects the phenotype.
- **Darwin and Wallace** developed the theory of evolution by natural selection **independently**.
- The theory was slow to be accepted: it conflicted with **religious beliefs**, and there was **no known mechanism of inheritance**.
- Natural selection, step 1: **there is genetic variation within the population**.
- Step 2: **organisms compete for limited resources, and more are produced than can survive**.
- Step 3: **those with characteristics best suited to the environment are more likely to survive and reproduce**.
- Step 4: **they pass on the alleles for those characteristics, so they become more common over generations**.
- Selection **selects from** existing variation — it does not **create** the characteristic.
- Say **more likely to survive**, never **in order to**.
- **Antibiotic resistance**: a **chance mutation** made some bacteria resistant **before** the antibiotic was used.
- The antibiotic **kills the non-resistant**, leaving the resistant to reproduce.
- It **selects**; it does not **cause** resistance.
- Resistance supports Darwin because every step is visible, over **days** rather than millennia.

options: Only plants are capable of evolving
Individuals cannot carry any mutations at all
Evolution is a change in a population over generations
Evolution requires the environment to stay constant for years
questions.solution: An individual is born with its alleles and keeps them. What changes is the **proportion of individuals in a population** carrying a particular allele, and that change happens **across generations** — so evolution is a property of **populations**, not of individuals.

questions.prompt: Darwin could describe that characteristics are inherited but not how. Why not?

Genes and DNA had not yet been discovered

questions.solution: **Genes, chromosomes and DNA were unknown**, and Mendel's work was not yet recognised. Darwin could show **that** offspring resemble their parents and that variation exists, but had no account of the **mechanism** — which, along with the religious objections, is why the theory was slow to be accepted.

questions.prompt: Why should a course of antibiotics be completed even once the patient feels better?
options: The antibiotic only works after the full course is taken
Any surviving bacteria are the most resistant and would reproduce
Stopping early causes new mutations to occur in the patient

questions.solution: Feeling better means most bacteria are dead — but the ones **most likely to have survived** are those with the **greatest resistance**. questions.prompt: Explain Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection, using antibiotic resistance in bacteria as an example.
questions.solution:
**Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection** follows four steps.

**First, there is genetic variation within a population.** This arises from **mutation**, which produces new alleles, and from **sexual reproduction**, which shuffles existing alleles into new combinations. The variation must be **already present** — this is the step most often left out.

**Second, organisms compete for limited resources.** More offspring are produced than can possibly survive, and food, space, light and mates are finite.

**Third, those individuals with characteristics best suited to the environment are more likely to survive and reproduce.** The wording matters: they are **more likely** to survive, not guaranteed to, and they do not develop the characteristic **in order to** survive.

**Fourth, the survivors pass on the alleles** for those characteristics, so those alleles become **more common in the population over generations**.

**Antibiotic resistance follows exactly this pattern.**

**Variation**: within a population of bacteria, a **random mutation** gives a small number of individuals resistance to a particular antibiotic. This happens **by chance**, and **before the antibiotic is ever used**.

**Selection pressure**: when the antibiotic is administered it creates an extremely strong selection pressure — an environment in which one characteristic alone decides survival.

**Differential survival**: the **non-resistant bacteria are killed**. The resistant ones **survive**.

**Inheritance**: the survivors **reproduce**, and bacteria do so very rapidly. They **pass on the allele for resistance**, so the population rebuilds — and every member of it is now resistant.

The numbers show how quickly this happens. If **1000** bacteria include just **1%** — **10** individuals — that are resistant, the antibiotic kills **990**. Those 10 then divide, and after only **7** generations there are $10 \times 2^7 = \mathbf{1280}$ bacteria: **more than the original population**, and **entirely resistant**. The proportion carrying the allele has gone from **1% to 100%**.

**Why this supports Darwin's theory** is that **every step can be observed**, and over **days** rather than the vast timescales usually involved. Fossils show that evolution has happened; antibiotic resistance shows it happening, with the mechanism visible.

**One error must be avoided.** The antibiotic did **not cause** the resistance. The resistant bacteria **already existed**; the antibiotic simply **removed their competition**. It **selects**, it does not create — and that distinction is the whole point of natural selection.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between genetic and environmental variation, and explain why only one of them can lead to evolution.
questions.solution:
The specification names **two causes of variation that influence phenotype**.

**Genetic variation** is **different characteristics as a result of mutation and sexual reproduction**.

**Mutations** are changes in the DNA, and they are the **original source** of all new alleles. Most have **no effect** on the phenotype, some have a **small** effect, and **rarely** a single mutation significantly affects it — so mutation supplies a steady trickle of new variants, most of which do nothing.

**Sexual reproduction** then **shuffles** those alleles. Meiosis produces genetically different gametes by sharing the chromosomes out differently, and two parents each contribute, so every offspring is a **new combination** of existing alleles. Sexual reproduction does not create new alleles, but it creates new **combinations** of them.

Together these mean there is usually **extensive genetic variation within a population of a species**.

**Environmental variation** is **different characteristics caused by an organism's environment** — what are called **acquired characteristics**.

Examples include a **scar** from an injury, **muscle** built by training, a **language** learned at school, or a plant that grows small because it was in poor soil or shade. All of these arise during the organism's **lifetime** as a result of what happens to it.

**Many characteristics involve both.** A person's height has a strong genetic component but is also affected by nutrition during childhood; two people with identical genes could end up different heights.

**Why only genetic variation can lead to evolution.** Natural selection works by a **characteristic being passed to offspring**. The chain is: individuals with a useful characteristic are **more likely to survive and reproduce**, and they **pass on the alleles** for it, so those alleles become **more common over generations**.

That chain requires the characteristic to be **heritable**. **Genetic** variation is carried in the **DNA of the gametes**, so it is passed to offspring and the chain works.

**Acquired characteristics are not inherited.** Building muscle through training changes the body, but it does **not change the alleles in the gametes**, so the offspring are born no more muscular than they would otherwise have been. However strongly an acquired characteristic helps an individual survive, it **cannot become more common in the next generation**, because there is no way for it to be transmitted.

This is why selection acts on **genetic variation alone**, and it is also why an important historical alternative — the idea that characteristics acquired during life are passed on — was abandoned. The mechanism of inheritance simply does not allow it, though Darwin himself could not have explained why, since **genes and DNA were unknown** in his lifetime.

**Mutations** are changes in the DNA, and they are the **original source** of all new alleles. Most have **no effect** on the phenotype, some have a **small** effect, and **rarely** a single mutation significantly affects it — so mutation supplies a steady trickle of new variants, most of which do nothing.

**Sexual reproduction** then **shuffles** those alleles. Meiosis produces genetically different gametes by sharing the chromosomes out differently, and two parents each contribute, so every offspring is a **new combination** of existing alleles. Sexual reproduction does not create new alleles, but it creates new **combinations** of them.

Together these mean there is usually **extensive genetic variation within a population of a species**.

**Environmental variation** is **different characteristics caused by an organism's environment** — what are called **acquired characteristics**.

Examples include a **scar** from an injury, **muscle** built by training, a **language** learned at school, or a plant that grows small because it was in poor soil or shade. All of these arise during the organism's **lifetime** as a result of what happens to it.

**Many characteristics involve both.** A person's height has a strong genetic component but is also affected by nutrition during childhood; two people with identical genes could end up different heights.

**Why only genetic variation can lead to evolution.** Natural selection works by a **characteristic being passed to offspring**. The chain is: individuals with a useful characteristic are **more likely to survive and reproduce**, and they **pass on the alleles** for it, so those alleles become **more common over generations**.

That chain requires the characteristic to be **heritable**. **Genetic** variation is carried in the **DNA of the gametes**, so it is passed to offspring and the chain works.

**Acquired characteristics are not inherited.** Building muscle through training changes the body, but it does **not change the alleles in the gametes**, so the offspring are born no more muscular than they would otherwise have been. However strongly an acquired characteristic helps an individual survive, it **cannot become more common in the next generation**, because there is no way for it to be transmitted.

This is why selection acts on **genetic variation alone**, and it is also why an important historical alternative — the idea that characteristics acquired during life are passed on — was abandoned. The mechanism of inheritance simply does not allow it, though Darwin himself could not have explained why, since **genes and DNA were unknown** in his lifetime.

questions.prompt:
The table gives example figures for the percentage of samples of one type of bacterium, taken in a hospital, that were resistant to an antibiotic.

| Year | Samples resistant (%) |
| --- | --- |
| 2010 | 4 |
| 2012 | 9 |
| 2014 | 17 |
| 2016 | 30 |

How many times greater was the percentage of resistant samples in 2016 than in 2010?
questions.solution: $30 \div 4 = $ **7.5**, so the percentage was 7.5 times greater. Each use of the antibiotic kills non-resistant bacteria and leaves the resistant ones to reproduce, so the **proportion** carrying the resistance allele rises year on year.

examTechnique.body:
Put **variation first**: selection **selects from** existing variation rather than creating it. Say **more likely to survive**, never **in order to**.

For antibiotic resistance, state that the **mutation came first** and the antibiotic **kills the non-resistant** — it selects, it does not cause. Finish the chain with the **alleles being passed on**.
examinerErrors: Saying organisms develop characteristics "in order to" survive.
Saying the antibiotic causes the resistance.
Omitting that variation must exist before selection can act.
Stopping at "the resistant ones survive" without inheritance.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer begins with **variation**, caused by **mutation and sexual reproduction**, and never lets selection create the characteristic. It uses **more likely to survive** throughout, avoiding any hint of purpose. On antibiotic resistance it states plainly that the resistant bacteria **existed before** the antibiotic and that the antibiotic **removed their competition** — selecting, not causing — and it finishes the chain with the **allele being passed on** so the proportion rises. It credits **Wallace** alongside Darwin, explains why the theory was **slow to be accepted**, through religious objections and the **missing mechanism**, keeps **acquired characteristics** out of the argument, and remembers that it is **populations**, not individuals, that evolve.
